props.title: Ice Age
props.initialSlug: Prehistoric misfits unite to save a human baby

sections.content: Ice Age (2002) revolutionized animated prehistoric adventures by blending slapstick comedy with genuine heart. Blue Sky Studios crafted a winning formula: pair Ray Romano's deadpan woolly mammoth Manny with John Leguizamo's hyperactive sloth Sid and Denis Leary's conflicted saber-toothed tiger Diego. The film sparked a wildly successful franchise, but the original stands out for its perfect balance of humor and emotional depth. It followed DreamWorks' Shrek (2001) in proving animated films could succeed with sophisticated wit that worked for both kids and adults.

sections.content: The success of Ice Age helped establish Blue Sky Studios as a major player in animation, alongside Pixar and DreamWorks. While Pixar was pushing technical boundaries with Finding Nemo (2003) and The Incredibles (2004), Blue Sky found its niche with character-driven comedy and accessible storytelling. The studio's signature style - slightly cartoonier than Pixar but more grounded than DreamWorks - influenced later films like Robots (2005) and Horton Hears a Who! (2008).

Scrat, the acorn-obsessed squirrel, became an iconic character despite having no dialogue. His slapstick misadventures, inspired by classic Chuck Jones cartoons like Road Runner (1949), provided perfect comic relief between the main story beats. This character went on to star in several short films and became the mascot of Blue Sky Studios. The character's universal appeal demonstrated how physical comedy could transcend language barriers. sections.content: Ice Age's success in 2002 came at a crucial moment for computer animation. While Pixar had established the gold standard with Toy Story (1995), Ice Age proved there was room for different visual styles and tones. The film's character designs balanced caricature with believability - creating prehistoric animals that could emote clearly while maintaining their animal nature. This influenced later animated films like Madagascar (2005) and Over the Hedge (2006).
